Over time, this leads to inflammation, bone loss, and eventually tooth loss. The Two-Part Process: Scaling involves the careful removal of plaque, tartar, and bacterial toxins from the tooth surfaces, especially below the gum line and in periodontal pockets.Root Planing smooths root surfaces, helping the gums reattach to the teeth and making it harder for bacteria to accumulate again. This treatment helps stop the progression of gum disease, promotes healing, and reduces the depth of periodontal pockets.

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain veneers are ultra-thin, custom-crafted shells of dental ceramic bonded to the front surfaces of your teeth. In a single treatment plan, they can correct the color, shape, size, and minor alignment of your smile — covering chips and cracks, closing small gaps, evening out short or worn teeth, and masking deep discoloration that whitening cannot fix. Many of our Korean-speaking patients know them as 라미네이트 (laminate veneers) — the same treatment, held to the same exacting standard of natural-looking results.Because porcelain reflects light the way natural enamel does, a well-made veneer is indistinguishable from a healthy natural tooth. The difference between a smile that looks "done" and one that simply looks beautiful comes down to design — which is why every veneer case at ID Dental starts with a full digital smile design, not a shade guide and a guess.

All-on-4 is a revolutionary implant technique that uses just four strategically placed titanium implants to support an entire arch of teeth. By angling the two back implants, Dr. Nam can maximize contact with available bone — even in patients with some bone loss — often eliminating the need for bone grafting.The result is a fixed, non-removable arch of teeth that looks and functions like your natural teeth. Unlike dentures, All-on-4 implants are permanent — they do not slip, click, or require adhesives.At ID Dental Implant Center, many All-on-4 patients receive a temporary arch of teeth on the same day as their implant surgery, so they leave the office smiling.

▸Missing most or all teeth on one or both arches▸Wearing uncomfortable, loose dentures▸Significant decay requiring full extraction▸Some bone loss (often still treatable without grafting)▸Good overall health (non-smoker preferred)

acceptedAnswer.text: While All-on-4 uses four implants to support a full arch, All-on-6 uses six implants — typically all placed at perpendicular (not angled) positions. Signs You May Need a Root Canal

An infected or inflamed tooth pulp rarely heals on its own. Catching it early lets Dr. Nam save the tooth before the infection spreads. Watch for these common signs — and call us promptly if any of them sound familiar.
Deep, throbbing pain that lingers or returns — especially when chewing or applying pressure.
Sharp pain that lingers long after eating or drinking something hot or cold, rather than fading quickly.
Tenderness or swelling in the gums near the tooth, sometimes with a small pimple-like bump that may drain.
A tooth that turns gray or discolored can signal that the inner pulp is dying or already infected.
Deep decay or a cracked tooth
Large cavities, a lost filling, or a crack can expose the pulp to bacteria and lead to infection.Comfortable & Modern
Dr. Nam examines the tooth and takes X-rays to pinpoint the infection and map the canal anatomy before treatment begins.
The tooth is fully numbed with local anesthesia. The infected pulp is gently removed and the canal is disinfected and shaped.

A root canal is performed when the inner pulp of a tooth becomes infected or inflamed — often due to deep decay, a crack, or trauma. The procedure removes the infected tissue, cleans and shapes the canal, and seals the tooth to prevent re-infection. Despite its reputation, modern root canals are no more uncomfortable than a filling.Root canal therapy saves your natural tooth — which is always preferable to extraction. After treatment, the tooth is protected with a crown to restore full strength and function.

In some cases, a standard root canal is not sufficient — particularly when an infection persists after prior treatment, or when the canal anatomy is too complex to treat conventionally. An apicoectomy is a minor surgical procedure that removes the tip of the tooth root and the surrounding infected tissue.Endodontic surgery is a last resort before extraction — giving patients another opportunity to save a tooth that has already had root canal treatment.

Signs You May Need a Root Canal

An infected or inflamed tooth pulp rarely heals on its own. Catching it early lets Dr. Nam save the tooth before the infection spreads. Watch for these common signs — and call us promptly if any of them sound familiar.
Deep, throbbing pain that lingers or returns — especially when chewing or applying pressure.
Sharp pain that lingers long after eating or drinking something hot or cold, rather than fading quickly.
Tenderness or swelling in the gums near the tooth, sometimes with a small pimple-like bump that may drain.
A tooth that turns gray or discolored can signal that the inner pulp is dying or already infected.
Deep decay or a cracked tooth
Large cavities, a lost filling, or a crack can expose the pulp to bacteria and lead to infection.Comfortable & Modern
Dr. Nam examines the tooth and takes X-rays to pinpoint the infection and map the canal anatomy before treatment begins.
The tooth is fully numbed with local anesthesia. The infected pulp is gently removed and the canal is disinfected and shaped.

A root canal is performed when the inner pulp of a tooth becomes infected or inflamed — often due to deep decay, a crack, or trauma. The procedure removes the infected tissue, cleans and shapes the canal, and seals the tooth to prevent re-infection. Despite its reputation, modern root canals are no more uncomfortable than a filling.Root canal therapy saves your natural tooth — which is always preferable to extraction. After treatment, the tooth is protected with a crown to restore full strength and function.

In some cases, a standard root canal is not sufficient — particularly when an infection persists after prior treatment, or when the canal anatomy is too complex to treat conventionally. An apicoectomy is a minor surgical procedure that removes the tip of the tooth root and the surrounding infected tissue.Endodontic surgery is a last resort before extraction — giving patients another opportunity to save a tooth that has already had root canal treatment.

How long does All-on-4 surgery take?
The surgical procedure typically takes 2–4 hours per arch. Many patients receive temporary teeth the same day. The final permanent arch is placed after osseointegration (3–6 months).
All-on-6 vs All-on-4: What's the Difference?

While All-on-4 uses four implants to support a full arch, All-on-6 uses six implants — typically all placed at perpendicular (not angled) positions. This additional support distributes biting forces more evenly across the jaw, which can be particularly advantageous for patients with higher bite forces, broader arches, or greater bone density.All-on-6 is often considered the premium option for full-arch restoration: the additional implants provide a more solid foundation, distribute load more evenly, and may reduce stress on individual implants over time.

Full mouth restoration refers to the comprehensive reconstruction of all or most teeth using a combination of implants, crowns, bridges, and other restorations. It is designed for patients with extensive tooth loss, severe decay, or structural damage affecting most of their teeth.Unlike All-on-4 or All-on-6 (which provide a fixed arch on 4 or 6 implants), full mouth restoration may involve individual implants, implant-supported bridges, and crowns placed throughout the mouth — creating the most natural result possible when full-arch solutions are not ideal.Dr. Nam will design a comprehensive treatment plan that addresses your specific situation — often combining extractions, bone grafting, implant placement, and cosmetic finishing in a coordinated sequence.
